expectedText:
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS — CLAIMANT INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS CLAIMANT INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's unemployment insurance eligibility framework and claims process from the perspective of a claimant. Morgan T. Ellis's employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc. ended on March 14, 2026, and Morgan T. Ellis filed a claim for unemployment insurance benefits with the California Employment Development Department (EDD) on March 21, 2026. This document states facts about the eligibility conditions, disqualification standard, benefit-amount computation, appeal process, and certification obligations that California's Unemployment Insurance Code sets for a claimant generally. It does not determine that Morgan T. Ellis is or is not eligible for benefits, and it is not itself a claim, weekly certification, or appeal filed with the EDD.

WEEKLY ELIGIBILITY CONDITIONS
California law does not treat eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits as a one-time determination made when a claim is first filed. Instead, a statute sets out conditions a claimant must meet with respect to each individual week for which benefits are claimed. The director must find, for that week, that: a claim for benefits for that week was made in accordance with authorized regulations; the claimant has registered for work and continued to report at a public employment office or another approved place (a requirement that may be waived or altered by regulation for partially employed individuals attached to regular jobs); the claimant was able to work and available for work that week; the claimant has served the one-week waiting period defined in a separate statute addressed below, unless that waiting period was waived under a specific Government Code provision; the claimant conducted a search for suitable work in accordance with the specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office; and, if the claimant has been identified under an automated profiling system as likely to exhaust regular benefits, the claimant participated as required in reemployment activities such as orientation and assessment, absent a showing of good cause for not participating. Because this is a week-by-week standard, it is the statutory basis for the recurring duty to certify continued eligibility for each week claimed, including the duty to conduct the required work search, rather than a condition satisfied once at the start of a claim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An unemployed individual is eligible to receive unemployment compensation benefits with respect to any week only if the director finds that: (a) A claim for benefits with respect to that week has been made in accordance with authorized regulations. (b) He or she has registered for work, and thereafter continued to report, at a public employment office or any other place as the director may approve. Either or both of the requirements of this subdivision may be waived or altered by authorized regulation as to partially employed individuals attached to regular jobs. (c) He or she was able to work and available for work for that week. (d) He has been unemployed for a waiting period of one week as defined in Section 1254, unless this waiting period has been waived pursuant to Section 8571 of the Government Code. (e) He or she conducted a search for suitable work in accordance with specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office. (f) He or she participated as required by the director in reemployment activities, such as orientation and assessment if the individual has been identified pursuant to an automated profiling system as likely to exhaust regular unemployment benefits unless the individual has shown good cause for failure to participate."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1253 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1253.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1253), used as real evidence of the recurring, week-by-week eligibility framework a state can build into its unemployment insurance system — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's situation, and not a determination that any specific claimant has or has not met these conditions for any given week. This clause quotes the whole of § 1253 as a single source; it cites only this one statutory section, so the multiple-subsection disclosure required elsewhere in this document does not apply here. The statute's subdivision (e) requires a work search 'in accordance with specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office' — a narrower, instruction-dependent formulation than a generic phrase like 'actively seeking work' might suggest, and this document does not describe what specific instructions any public employment office has issued or would issue to any particular claimant. This document does not itself file a claim, certify a week, or determine that any of these conditions is or is not met for any specific claimant.

THE ONE-WEEK WAITING PERIOD
One of the eligibility conditions described above requires the claimant to have served a waiting period of one week, and a separate statute defines what that means. A week does not count toward this waiting period unless it falls within the benefit year that includes the week for which the claimant seeks payment (though this rule does not interrupt payment for consecutive weeks of unemployment, and a week immediately before a benefit year can, in some circumstances, be treated as within it); a week does not count if benefits have already been paid for it; and a week does not count unless the claimant was otherwise eligible for that week in all respects apart from the waiting-period requirement itself and a separate statute on partial and part-time earnings.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No week shall be counted as a week of unemployment under subdivision (d) of Section 1253: (a) Unless it occurs within the benefit year which includes the week with respect to which he claims payment of unemployment compensation benefits, but this requirement shall not interrupt the payment of such benefits for consecutive weeks of unemployment. The week immediately preceding a benefit year, if part of one uninterrupted period of unemployment which continues into that benefit year shall be deemed, for the purposes of this section only, to be within such benefit year as well as within the preceding benefit year. (b) If unemployment compensation benefits have been paid with respect to that week. (c) Unless the individual was eligible for unemployment compensation benefits with respect thereto in all respects, except for the requirements of subdivision (d) of Section 1253 and Section 1281."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1254 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1254.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1254), used as real evidence that California's waiting period is one week — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's timeline, and not a statement about how many weeks any particular claimant has actually served. This document's drafter was initially asked to verify whether Unemployment Insurance Code § 1030 or § 1032 sets the waiting period. Neither does: both sections were checked directly and are unrelated to the waiting period — § 1030 sets the employer's window to submit facts on the separation issue described in a later clause, and § 1032 governs whether benefit charges are excluded from an employer's reserve account. The real source is § 1253(d), which requires the waiting period, together with § 1254, which defines it — both checked directly for this clause. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1254); no additional independent source was found for this. This document does not calculate how many, if any, waiting-period weeks any specific claimant has served.

DISQUALIFICATION FOR VOLUNTARILY QUITTING WITHOUT GOOD CAUSE OR DISCHARGE FOR MISCONDUCT
Separately from the weekly conditions above, a claimant is disqualified from benefits if the director finds that the claimant left the most recent work voluntarily without good cause, or was discharged for misconduct connected with that work. The same statute creates a rebuttable presumption running in the claimant's favor: a claimant is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct, and not to have voluntarily left without good cause, unless the employer has given the EDD written notice to the contrary, setting out facts sufficient to overcome that presumption. Neither 'good cause' nor 'misconduct' is defined in general terms within the statute. The same statute does, however, deem certain specific circumstances to be good cause as a matter of law, including leaving employment to accompany or join a spouse or domestic partner at a place from which commuting is impractical, and leaving employment to protect oneself or one's family from domestic violence abuse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An individual is disqualified for unemployment compensation benefits if the director finds that he or she left his or her most recent work voluntarily without good cause or that he or she has been discharged for misconduct connected with his or her most recent work. An individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct in connection with his or her work and not to have voluntarily left his or her work without good cause unless his or her employer has given written notice to the contrary to the department as provided in Section 1327, setting forth facts sufficient to overcome the presumption. The presumption provided by this section is rebuttable."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1256.)
  "An individual may be deemed to have left his or her most recent work with good cause if he or she leaves employment to accompany his or her spouse or domestic partner to a place or to join him or her at a place from which it is impractical to commute to the employment. For purposes of this section “spouse” includes a person to whom marriage is imminent, and “domestic partner” includes a person to whom a domestic partnership, as described in Section 297 of the Family Code, is imminent. An individual may be deemed to have left his or her most recent work with good cause if he or she leaves employment to protect his or her family, or himself or herself, from domestic violence abuse."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1256.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256), used as real evidence of the substantive disqualification standard, the burden-shifting presumption, and the specific statutory good-cause categories a state can attach to a claimant's reason for separation — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's eligibility, and not a characterization of any specific claimant's own separation. This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory section (§ 1256): the general disqualification-and-presumption paragraph, and the paragraph deeming certain circumstances to be good cause. These two quotations are being treated as one source, not as independent corroborating sources, because they come from the same statutory section. This is also the same statutory section already cited, for the employer-facing side of this same disqualification question, by this corpus's Employer's Response to Unemployment Insurance Claim document (its uiresponse_disqualification_standard clause); that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as a second, independent source — this clause states the identical statutory standard from the claimant's own perspective and does not add independent verification beyond what that document already established. Beyond the specific circumstances the statute itself deems to be good cause, the general terms 'good cause' and 'misconduct' have been the subject of substantial EDD precedent decisions and California appellate case law. This document's drafter attempted to locate and verify a citable, on-point California appellate decision construing one of these terms, but the CourtListener research tool used for that purpose returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before any search could be completed in this session. Rather than invent or rely on an unverified case citation, this document discloses that limitation honestly and does not cite any case law on the meaning of 'good cause' or 'misconduct.' This document does not itself determine that any specific claimant's own separation from a specific employer does or does not meet this standard.

HOW CALIFORNIA COURTS DEFINE "MISCONDUCT": AMADOR V. UNEMPLOYMENT INS. APPEALS BD.
Because Section 1256 does not itself define "misconduct," California courts have supplied the definition. The leading California Supreme Court decision construing the term, Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671, adopted and applied a definition originating in the Court of Appeal's decision in Maywood Glass Co. v. Stewart (1959) 170 Cal.App.2d 719: disqualifying misconduct is conduct evincing willful or wanton disregard of the employer's interests, shown in deliberate violation of standards of behavior the employer has the right to expect, or in carelessness or negligence of a degree or recurrence manifesting equal culpability, wrongful intent, or evil design, or an intentional and substantial disregard of the employer's interests or the employee's duties. On the other side of that line, the same definition states that mere inefficiency, unsatisfactory conduct, failure in good performance due to inability or incapacity, isolated inadvertencies or ordinary negligence, or good-faith errors in judgment or discretion are not "misconduct" within the meaning of the statute. The Amador court also traced this distinction to the code's own stated policy of providing benefits to "persons unemployed through no fault of their own," describing fault as the basic element in interpreting and applying the misconduct disqualification. Applying this standard to the facts before it, the Amador court held that a hospital employee who was discharged for willfully refusing to perform a procedure she reasonably and in good faith believed would jeopardize patient health had not committed "misconduct" within the meaning of Section 1256.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The term “misconduct,” as used in the code, is limited to “ ‘conduct evincing such wilful or wanton disregard of an employer’s interests as is found in deliberate violations or disregard of standards of behavior which the employer has the right to expect of his employee, or in carelessness or negligence of such degree or recurrence as to manifest equal culpability, wrongful intent or evil design, or to show an intentional and substantial disregard of the employer’s interests or of the employee’s duties and obligations to his employer. On the other hand mere inefficiency, unsatisfactory conduct, failure in good performance as the result of inability or incapacity, inadvertencies or ordinary negligence in isolated instances, or good faith errors in judgment or discretion are not to be deemed “misconduct” within the meaning of the statute.’ ”"
  — Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984), 35 Cal.3d 671, 677 P.2d 224, 200 Cal.Rptr. 298 (1984) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1308295/amador-v-unemployment-insurance-appeals-board/)
  "The policy of the code is to provide benefits to “persons unemployed through no fault of their own.” (§ 100.) “Accordingly, fault is the basic element to be considered in interpreting and applying the code sections on unemployment compensation.” ... [T]his court holds that a worker who has been discharged for wilfully refusing to perform work which she reasonably and in good faith believed would jeopardize the health of others has not committed “misconduct” within the meaning of section 1256."
  — Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984), 35 Cal.3d 671, 677 P.2d 224, 200 Cal.Rptr. 298 (1984) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1308295/amador-v-unemployment-insurance-appeals-board/)
  Known gap: This document's drafter located Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671 via CourtListener, confirmed its citation (35 Cal.3d 671, 677 P.2d 224, 200 Cal.Rptr. 298), and read the opinion's full text (CourtListener opinion id 9571860) before treating any holding or quotation from it as verified. Only Amador's own opinion was read and independently confirmed. The Maywood Glass Co. v. Stewart definition, and the code-policy "fault" language, are both block-quoted inside the Amador opinion rather than independently pulled from Maywood Glass Co.'s own opinion or from the Rowe v. Hansen decision Amador cites for the "fault" point; this document attributes those quotations to Amador (which itself quotes them) rather than implying independent verification of Maywood Glass Co. or Rowe. This document does not apply this standard to, or draw any conclusion about, any specific claimant's own conduct or separation.

HOW "GOOD CAUSE" CASE LAW RELATES TO THE MISCONDUCT STANDARD
Although Section 1256 states voluntary quit without good cause and discharge for misconduct as separate disqualifying grounds, Amador observed that case law on one informs the other: if a claimant's reasons for refusing a work directive would constitute good cause sufficient to justify resigning outright, those same reasons should also justify the less drastic step of refusing that particular work assignment, so that a discharge for such a refusal is not "misconduct." On the general meaning of "good cause" itself, Amador reiterated that the concept cannot be arbitrarily limited, and that it must account for real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith. Amador also noted, as a general principle limiting misconduct disqualifications, that a claimant may not be denied benefits solely on the basis of a good-faith error in judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Although this case involves a discharge for “misconduct,” the law concerning voluntary terminations for “good cause” is also relevant. If a claimant’s reasons for refusing work constitute “good cause” sufficient to justify resignation, it follows that they should also justify the less drastic step of refusing a work assignment."
  — Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984), 35 Cal.3d 671, 677 P.2d 224, 200 Cal.Rptr. 298 (1984) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1308295/amador-v-unemployment-insurance-appeals-board/)
  "A claimant may not be denied benefits solely on the basis of a “good faith error in judgment.” ... the concept of ‘good cause’ cannot be arbitrarily limited; the board must take account of ‘ “real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, palpable forces that operate to produce correlative results, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith.’ ”"
  — Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984), 35 Cal.3d 671, 677 P.2d 224, 200 Cal.Rptr. 298 (1984) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1308295/amador-v-unemployment-insurance-appeals-board/)
  Known gap: As with the preceding clause, this document's drafter read and independently confirmed Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671 via CourtListener (opinion id 9571860) before treating any quotation from it as verified; this clause is not an independent source from the preceding clause, since both quote the same opinion. The good-cause formulation quoted here is itself a passage Amador quotes from Gibson v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 494, which in turn quotes California Portland Cement Co. v. California Unemployment Ins. Appeals Board (1960) 178 Cal.App.2d 263; and the good-faith-error-in-judgment principle is a passage Amador quotes from Delgado v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1974) 41 Cal.App.3d 788. This document's drafter did not independently pull and verify the Gibson, California Portland Cement, or Delgado opinions themselves via CourtListener, and so does not cite them as independently verified sources; both quotations here are attributed to Amador, the opinion actually read, rather than to the cases Amador is quoting. This document does not apply this standard to, or draw any conclusion about, any specific claimant's own reasons for leaving or refusing work.

HOW THE WEEKLY BENEFIT AMOUNT IS CALCULATED, AND ITS STATUTORY MAXIMUM
A separate statute sets how a claimant's weekly benefit amount is computed. For a claim filed with an effective date on or after January 1, 2003, the weekly benefit amount is the figure appearing on a statutory wage-bracket table opposite the wage range that includes the wages the claimant was paid during the highest-earning quarter of the claimant's base period. For a claimant whose highest-quarter wages exceed the top of that table, the statute instead sets the weekly benefit amount at 50 percent of those wages divided by 13 — but caps that calculation at a fixed dollar maximum keyed to when the claim was filed. For any claim filed on or after January 1, 2005, that statutory maximum is $450 per week.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the amount of wages paid an individual for employment by employers exceeds one thousand eight hundred thirty-two dollars and ninety-nine cents ($1,832.99) in the quarter of his or her base period in which these wages were highest, the individual’s weekly benefit amount shall be 50 percent of these wages divided by 13, but in no case shall this amount exceed the applicable of the following: (1) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2003, and before January 1, 2004, three hundred seventy dollars ($370). (2) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2004, and before January 1, 2005, four hundred ten dollars ($410). (3) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2005, four hundred fifty dollars ($450). If the benefit payable under this subdivision is not a multiple of one dollar ($1), it shall be computed to the next higher multiple of one dollar ($1)."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1280(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1280.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1280(c)), used as real evidence of how California computes a weekly benefit amount and sets its statutory cap — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's benefit amount, and not a calculation of any specific claimant's actual weekly benefit amount, which depends on that claimant's own base-period wages and is not computed here. This document's drafter was asked to verify, rather than assume, whether the maximum weekly benefit amount is a fixed statutory dollar figure or a periodically adjusted one. Having checked the statute directly, the honest answer is that it is a fixed dollar figure written directly into the statutory text — $450 for any claim filed on or after January 1, 2005 — and that figure has not been amended since then; as of the date this clause was checked, it has remained $450 for roughly two decades notwithstanding intervening inflation, rather than adjusting automatically or periodically. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1280(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. Section 1280(c) also incorporates a lengthy numeric wage-bracket table with many lines; this clause quotes the subsection's operative capping sentence and does not reproduce that table.

THE EDD'S DETERMINATION AND THE CLAIMANT'S RIGHT TO APPEAL
After considering any facts an employer has submitted, the EDD must make a determination on the claimant's eligibility for benefits and must promptly notify the claimant, and any employer who submitted facts, of that determination and the reasons for it. Both the claimant and the employer may appeal a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of the notice — a deadline that may be extended for good cause, defined to include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The EDD's director is treated as an interested party to any such appeal. If the administrative law judge's decision is adverse, a further appeal may be taken to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board, again within 30 days after the decision is mailed (also extendable for good cause).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The department shall consider the facts submitted by an employer pursuant to Section 1327 and make a determination as to the claimant’s eligibility for benefits. The department shall promptly notify the claimant and any employer who before the determination has submitted facts or given notice pursuant to Section 1327 or this section and authorized regulations of the determination or reconsidered determination and the reasons therefor. If, after notice of a determination or reconsidered determination, the employing unit acquires knowledge of facts that may affect the eligibility of the claimant and those facts could not reasonably have been known within the 10-day period provided by Section 1327, the employing unit shall within 10 days of acquiring that knowledge submit those facts to the department, and the 10-day period may be extended for good cause. The claimant and the employer may appeal from a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of notice of the determination or reconsidered determination. The 30-day period may be extended for good cause, which shall include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The director shall be an interested party to any appeal."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1328.)
  "An administrative law judge after affording a reasonable opportunity for fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside any determination that is appealed under this article. The claimant, the employer becoming a party to the appeal by submitting a protest or information pursuant to Sections 1326 to 1333, inclusive, of this article, and the director shall be promptly notified in writing of the administrative law judge’s decision, together with reasons for it. The decision shall be final unless, within 30 days after mailing of the decision, further appeal is initiated to the appeals board pursuant to Section 1336. The 30-day limitation may be extended for good cause."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1334.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1328(a) and 1334(a)), used as real evidence of the two-tier administrative appeal structure a state can build into its unemployment insurance determination process — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's appeal rights, and not a statement that any specific claimant has or should appeal any determination. These two citations come from different statutory sections, each addressing a distinct stage of the appeal process (the initial determination and first appeal under § 1328, and the administrative law judge's decision and further appeal under § 1334); they are not multiple citations to subsections of the same section. This appeal right belongs to the claimant and is a different statutory point from the employer's own 10-day window to submit facts after being notified of the claim, which this corpus's Employer's Response to Unemployment Insurance Claim document addresses separately under Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1327 and 1030(a) — those sections are not re-cited here because they govern a different actor and a different deadline. This document does not itself file, or advise any specific claimant to file, any appeal, and it does not state whether an appeal in any particular case would succeed.

CERTIFYING FOR BENEFITS: THE FALSE STATEMENT PROHIBITION AND ITS PENALTY
A separate chapter of the same code makes it a violation to willfully make a false statement or representation, to knowingly fail to disclose a material fact, or to use a false name, false Social Security number, or other false identification, in order to obtain, increase, reduce, or defeat any benefit or payment — whether for the maker or for someone else — under California's own unemployment compensation provisions or several listed federal allowance programs the EDD also administers. A different statute in the same chapter sets the penalty: except for a short list of other, more specific violations this provision does not apply to, a violation of the chapter is punishable by imprisonment in county jail for up to one year, or in state prison, by a fine of not more than $20,000, or by both the fine and imprisonment, at the court's discretion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is a violation of this chapter to willfully make a false statement or representation, to knowingly fail to disclose a material fact, or to use a false name, false social security number, or other false identification to obtain, increase, reduce, or defeat any benefit or payment, whether for the maker or for any other person, under any of the following statutes administered by the department: (1) The provisions of this division. (2) The provisions of any unemployment insurance law of the federal government. (3) The provisions of any training allowance law of the federal government. (4) The provisions of any trade readjustment allowance law of the federal government. (5) The provisions of any other allowance law of the federal government."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2101(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=2101.)
  "Except as provided in Sections 2117, 2117.5, 2118, and 2118.5, a violation of this chapter is punishable by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, or in the state prison, or by a fine of not more than twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), or by both the fine and imprisonment, at the discretion of the court."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2122 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=2122.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 2101(a) and 2122), used as real evidence that California attaches a real, sourced criminal penalty to a false statement made to obtain unemployment benefits — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant, and not a statement that any specific claimant has made, or has not made, a false statement. These two citations come from different statutory sections: § 2101(a) defines the violation, and § 2122 is a separate, general penalty provision for Chapter 10 violations that is needed because § 2101 itself does not state a punishment; they are not multiple citations to subsections of the same section. Section 2122 excludes a short list of other violations (Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 2117, 2117.5, 2118, and 2118.5) that carry their own, separately stated penalties; those sections concern employer tax-withholding and reporting violations rather than a claimant's false statement under § 2101, and this document does not address them further. This document's drafter also looked for, but did not find, a standalone Unemployment Insurance Code section imposing a freestanding duty to report earnings while certifying for benefits, separate from the general authority to set claims-filing regulations in Section 1326 and the false-statement-and-nondisclosure prohibition quoted above; unreported earnings that should have been disclosed would fall within that prohibition's 'knowingly fail to disclose a material fact' language rather than a separately numbered earnings-reporting statute, so far as this document's research located. This document does not itself constitute a certification for benefits, and does not state that any specific claimant has violated, or complied with, this prohibition.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Morgan T. Ellis acknowledges having received and reviewed this information sheet regarding California's unemployment insurance eligibility framework and claims process, in connection with the claim Morgan T. Ellis filed with the EDD on March 21, 2026 following the end of Morgan T. Ellis's employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc. on March 14, 2026. This document is informational only. It does not itself constitute a claim, weekly certification, or appeal, and Morgan T. Ellis understands that any such filing must be made directly with the EDD.

Ellis's employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc. ended on March 14, 2026, and Morgan T. Ellis filed a claim for unemployment insurance benefits with the California Employment Development Department (EDD) on March 21, 2026. This document states facts about the eligibility conditions, disqualification standard, benefit-amount computation, appeal process, and certification obligations that California's Unemployment Insurance Code sets for a claimant generally. It does not determine that Morgan T. Ellis is or is not eligible for benefits, and it is not itself a claim, weekly certification, or appeal filed with the EDD.

California law does not treat eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits as a one-time determination made when a claim is first filed. Instead, a statute sets out conditions a claimant must meet with respect to each individual week for which benefits are claimed. The director must find, for that week, that: a claim for benefits for that week was made in accordance with authorized regulations; the claimant has registered for work and continued to report at a public employment office or another approved place (a requirement that may be waived or altered by regulation for partially employed individuals attached to regular jobs); the claimant was able to work and available for work that week; the claimant has served the one-week waiting period defined in a separate statute addressed below, unless that waiting period was waived under a specific Government Code provision; the claimant conducted a search for suitable work in accordance with the specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office; and, if the claimant has been identified under an automated profiling system as likely to exhaust regular benefits, the claimant participated as required in reemployment activities such as orientation and assessment, absent a showing of good cause for not participating. Because this is a week-by-week standard, it is the statutory basis for the recurring duty to certify continued eligibility for each week claimed, including the duty to conduct the required work search, rather than a condition satisfied once at the start of a claim.

expectedJSON.body: One of the eligibility conditions described above requires the claimant to have served a waiting period of one week, and a separate statute defines what that means. A week does not count toward this waiting period unless it falls within the benefit year that includes the week for which the claimant seeks payment (though this rule does not interrupt payment for consecutive weeks of unemployment, and a week immediately before a benefit year can, in some circumstances, be treated as within it); a week does not count if benefits have already been paid for it; and a week does not count unless the claimant was otherwise eligible for that week in all respects apart from the waiting-period requirement itself and a separate statute on partial and part-time earnings.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1254 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: No week shall be counted as a week of unemployment under subdivision (d) of Section 1253: (a) Unless it occurs within the benefit year which includes the week with respect to which he claims payment of unemployment compensation benefits, but this requirement shall not interrupt the payment of such benefits for consecutive weeks of unemployment. The week immediately preceding a benefit year, if part of one uninterrupted period of unemployment which continues into that benefit year shall be deemed, for the purposes of this section only, to be within such benefit year as well as within the preceding benefit year. (b) If unemployment compensation benefits have been paid with respect to that week. (c) Unless the individual was eligible for unemployment compensation benefits with respect thereto in all respects, except for the requirements of subdivision (d) of Section 1253 and Section 1281.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the weekly conditions above, a claimant is disqualified from benefits if the director finds that the claimant left the most recent work voluntarily without good cause, or was discharged for misconduct connected with that work. The same statute creates a rebuttable presumption running in the claimant's favor: a claimant is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct, and not to have voluntarily left without good cause, unless the employer has given the EDD written notice to the contrary, setting out facts sufficient to overcome that presumption. Neither 'good cause' nor 'misconduct' is defined in general terms within the statute. The same statute does, however, deem certain specific circumstances to be good cause as a matter of law, including leaving employment to accompany or join a spouse or domestic partner at a place from which commuting is impractical, and leaving employment to protect oneself or one's family from domestic violence abuse.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An individual is disqualified for unemployment compensation benefits if the director finds that he or she left his or her most recent work voluntarily without good cause or that he or she has been discharged for misconduct connected with his or her most recent work. An individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct in connection with his or her work and not to have voluntarily left his or her work without good cause unless his or her employer has given written notice to the contrary to the department as provided in Section 1327, setting forth facts sufficient to overcome the presumption. The presumption provided by this section is rebuttable.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An individual may be deemed to have left his or her most recent work with good cause if he or she leaves employment to accompany his or her spouse or domestic partner to a place or to join him or her at a place from which it is impractical to commute to the employment. For purposes of this section “spouse” includes a person to whom marriage is imminent, and “domestic partner” includes a person to whom a domestic partnership, as described in Section 297 of the Family Code, is imminent. An individual may be deemed to have left his or her most recent work with good cause if he or she leaves employment to protect his or her family, or himself or herself, from domestic violence abuse.

expectedJSON.body: Because Section 1256 does not itself define "misconduct," California courts have supplied the definition. The leading California Supreme Court decision construing the term, Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671, adopted and applied a definition originating in the Court of Appeal's decision in Maywood Glass Co. v. Stewart (1959) 170 Cal.App.2d 719: disqualifying misconduct is conduct evincing willful or wanton disregard of the employer's interests, shown in deliberate violation of standards of behavior the employer has the right to expect, or in carelessness or negligence of a degree or recurrence manifesting equal culpability, wrongful intent, or evil design, or an intentional and substantial disregard of the employer's interests or the employee's duties. On the other side of that line, the same definition states that mere inefficiency, unsatisfactory conduct, failure in good performance due to inability or incapacity, isolated inadvertencies or ordinary negligence, or good-faith errors in judgment or discretion are not "misconduct" within the meaning of the statute. The Amador court also traced this distinction to the code's own stated policy of providing benefits to "persons unemployed through no fault of their own," describing fault as the basic element in interpreting and applying the misconduct disqualification. Applying this standard to the facts before it, the Amador court held that a hospital employee who was discharged for willfully refusing to perform a procedure she reasonably and in good faith believed would jeopardize patient health had not committed "misconduct" within the meaning of Section 1256.

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: The term “misconduct,” as used in the code, is limited to “ ‘conduct evincing such wilful or wanton disregard of an employer’s interests as is found in deliberate violations or disregard of standards of behavior which the employer has the right to expect of his employee, or in carelessness or negligence of such degree or recurrence as to manifest equal culpability, wrongful intent or evil design, or to show an intentional and substantial disregard of the employer’s interests or of the employee’s duties and obligations to his employer. On the other hand mere inefficiency, unsatisfactory conduct, failure in good performance as the result of inability or incapacity, inadvertencies or ordinary negligence in isolated instances, or good faith errors in judgment or discretion are not to be deemed “misconduct” within the meaning of the statute.’ ”

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: The policy of the code is to provide benefits to “persons unemployed through no fault of their own.” (§ 100.) “Accordingly, fault is the basic element to be considered in interpreting and applying the code sections on unemployment compensation.” ... [T]his court holds that a worker who has been discharged for wilfully refusing to perform work which she reasonably and in good faith believed would jeopardize the health of others has not committed “misconduct” within the meaning of section 1256.

expectedJSON.body: Although Section 1256 states voluntary quit without good cause and discharge for misconduct as separate disqualifying grounds, Amador observed that case law on one informs the other: if a claimant's reasons for refusing a work directive would constitute good cause sufficient to justify resigning outright, those same reasons should also justify the less drastic step of refusing that particular work assignment, so that a discharge for such a refusal is not "misconduct." On the general meaning of "good cause" itself, Amador reiterated that the concept cannot be arbitrarily limited, and that it must account for real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith. Amador also noted, as a general principle limiting misconduct disqualifications, that a claimant may not be denied benefits solely on the basis of a good-faith error in judgment.

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: Although this case involves a discharge for “misconduct,” the law concerning voluntary terminations for “good cause” is also relevant. If a claimant’s reasons for refusing work constitute “good cause” sufficient to justify resignation, it follows that they should also justify the less drastic step of refusing a work assignment.

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: A claimant may not be denied benefits solely on the basis of a “good faith error in judgment.” ... the concept of ‘good cause’ cannot be arbitrarily limited; the board must take account of ‘ “real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, palpable forces that operate to produce correlative results, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith.’ ”

expectedJSON.body: A separate statute sets how a claimant's weekly benefit amount is computed. For a claim filed with an effective date on or after January 1, 2003, the weekly benefit amount is the figure appearing on a statutory wage-bracket table opposite the wage range that includes the wages the claimant was paid during the highest-earning quarter of the claimant's base period. For a claimant whose highest-quarter wages exceed the top of that table, the statute instead sets the weekly benefit amount at 50 percent of those wages divided by 13 — but caps that calculation at a fixed dollar maximum keyed to when the claim was filed. For any claim filed on or after January 1, 2005, that statutory maximum is $450 per week.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1280(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the amount of wages paid an individual for employment by employers exceeds one thousand eight hundred thirty-two dollars and ninety-nine cents ($1,832.99) in the quarter of his or her base period in which these wages were highest, the individual’s weekly benefit amount shall be 50 percent of these wages divided by 13, but in no case shall this amount exceed the applicable of the following: (1) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2003, and before January 1, 2004, three hundred seventy dollars ($370). (2) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2004, and before January 1, 2005, four hundred ten dollars ($410). (3) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2005, four hundred fifty dollars ($450). If the benefit payable under this subdivision is not a multiple of one dollar ($1), it shall be computed to the next higher multiple of one dollar ($1).

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1280(c)), used as real evidence of how California computes a weekly benefit amount and sets its statutory cap — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's benefit amount, and not a calculation of any specific claimant's actual weekly benefit amount, which depends on that claimant's own base-period wages and is not computed here. This document's drafter was asked to verify, rather than assume, whether the maximum weekly benefit amount is a fixed statutory dollar figure or a periodically adjusted one. Having checked the statute directly, the honest answer is that it is a fixed dollar figure written directly into the statutory text — $450 for any claim filed on or after January 1, 2005 — and that figure has not been amended since then; as of the date this clause was checked, it has remained $450 for roughly two decades notwithstanding intervening inflation, rather than adjusting automatically or periodically. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1280(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. Section 1280(c) also incorporates a lengthy numeric wage-bracket table with many lines; this clause quotes the subsection's operative capping sentence and does not reproduce that table.

expectedJSON.body: After considering any facts an employer has submitted, the EDD must make a determination on the claimant's eligibility for benefits and must promptly notify the claimant, and any employer who submitted facts, of that determination and the reasons for it. Both the claimant and the employer may appeal a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of the notice — a deadline that may be extended for good cause, defined to include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The EDD's director is treated as an interested party to any such appeal. If the administrative law judge's decision is adverse, a further appeal may be taken to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board, again within 30 days after the decision is mailed (also extendable for good cause).

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The department shall consider the facts submitted by an employer pursuant to Section 1327 and make a determination as to the claimant’s eligibility for benefits. The department shall promptly notify the claimant and any employer who before the determination has submitted facts or given notice pursuant to Section 1327 or this section and authorized regulations of the determination or reconsidered determination and the reasons therefor. If, after notice of a determination or reconsidered determination, the employing unit acquires knowledge of facts that may affect the eligibility of the claimant and those facts could not reasonably have been known within the 10-day period provided by Section 1327, the employing unit shall within 10 days of acquiring that knowledge submit those facts to the department, and the 10-day period may be extended for good cause. The claimant and the employer may appeal from a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of notice of the determination or reconsidered determination. The 30-day period may be extended for good cause, which shall include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The director shall be an interested party to any appeal.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An administrative law judge after affording a reasonable opportunity for fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside any determination that is appealed under this article. The claimant, the employer becoming a party to the appeal by submitting a protest or information pursuant to Sections 1326 to 1333, inclusive, of this article, and the director shall be promptly notified in writing of the administrative law judge’s decision, together with reasons for it. The decision shall be final unless, within 30 days after mailing of the decision, further appeal is initiated to the appeals board pursuant to Section 1336. The 30-day limitation may be extended for good cause.

These two citations come from different statutory sections, each addressing a distinct stage of the appeal process (the initial determination and first appeal under § 1328, and the administrative law judge's decision and further appeal under § 1334); they are not multiple citations to subsections of the same section. This appeal right belongs to the claimant and is a different statutory point from the employer's own 10-day window to submit facts after being notified of the claim, which this corpus's Employer's Response to Unemployment Insurance Claim document addresses separately under Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1327 and 1030(a) — those sections are not re-cited here because they govern a different actor and a different deadline. This document does not itself file, or advise any specific claimant to file, any appeal, and it does not state whether an appeal in any particular case would succeed.

expectedJSON.body: A separate chapter of the same code makes it a violation to willfully make a false statement or representation, to knowingly fail to disclose a material fact, or to use a false name, false Social Security number, or other false identification, in order to obtain, increase, reduce, or defeat any benefit or payment — whether for the maker or for someone else — under California's own unemployment compensation provisions or several listed federal allowance programs the EDD also administers. A different statute in the same chapter sets the penalty: except for a short list of other, more specific violations this provision does not apply to, a violation of the chapter is punishable by imprisonment in county jail for up to one year, or in state prison, by a fine of not more than $20,000, or by both the fine and imprisonment, at the court's discretion.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2101(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: It is a violation of this chapter to willfully make a false statement or representation, to knowingly fail to disclose a material fact, or to use a false name, false social security number, or other false identification to obtain, increase, reduce, or defeat any benefit or payment, whether for the maker or for any other person, under any of the following statutes administered by the department: (1) The provisions of this division. (2) The provisions of any unemployment insurance law of the federal government. (3) The provisions of any training allowance law of the federal government. (4) The provisions of any trade readjustment allowance law of the federal government. (5) The provisions of any other allowance law of the federal government.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2122 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 2117, 2117.5, 2118, and 2118.5, a violation of this chapter is punishable by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, or in the state prison, or by a fine of not more than twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), or by both the fine and imprisonment, at the discretion of the court.
